A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FedQ-Advantage and provide readable text, equations, figures, algorithms, and complete appendices. Their content can be matched reliably despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix B report original synthetic-MDP simulations comparing regret, communication rounds, and multi-agent speedup.

after.justification: Appendix C retains those simulations and adds results for two further synthetic-MDP configurations in Figure 4.

M1.justification: Originally, one agent reaching its threshold triggers termination for all agents. Section 3.2 and Algorithm 1 introduce usyn, allowing communication to wait until every agent independently reaches a threshold. This adds a substantive communication procedure while retaining the reference-advantage updates and stage design.

E1.justification: Appendix C.3 adds smaller and larger synthetic-MDP scenarios: (H,S,A)=(5,3,2) and (20,20,5), beyond the retained (10,5,5) environment. This modestly broadens coverage of environment sizes and episode horizons within the same tabular task family.

E2.justification: The federated comparisons retain FedQ-Hoeffding and FedQ-Bernstein, including in the additional experiments. The speedup comparison retains UCB-A with the same two episode budgets. Newly discussed related methods are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Figure 4 adds evaluations extending to 300,000 and 5,000,000 total episodes, as shown on its axes. The retained comparison uses 1,000,000 total episodes. These additional protocols retain the regret normalization and communication-round metrics.

E4.justification: Appendix C.3 adds a limited sensitivity check examining whether the comparative regret and communication behavior persists in smaller and larger MDPs. The existing multi-agent speedup analysis is retained.

E5.justification: The retained experiments still use ten sample paths, medians, and 10th–90th percentile bands. Appendix C.3 specifies ten replications for the smaller added environment and only one replication for the larger environment, whose curves have no uncertainty bands.

E6.justification: The original experimental plots are unchanged and become Figures 2–3. New Figure 4 adds regret and communication curves for two additional environments, with FedQ-Advantage finishing below FedQ-Hoeffding and FedQ-Bernstein on both measures. These are additional results under different settings.

T1.justification: Theorem 4.2 and Appendix F add a bound without forced synchronization, reducing communication cost from O(M^2 H^3 S^2 A log H log T) to O(M H^3 S^2 A log H log T). Theorem 4.1 explicitly covers both modes and sharpens its stated burn-in dependence on M. Appendices D–E also correct the coefficient in event E9 and its corresponding decomposition.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution summary elevate optional forced synchronization into a central contribution. Section 1.2 strengthens the communication claim through the new mode and its relationship to single-agent policy-switching bounds, while retaining the almost-optimal regret and near-linear speedup claims.

C2.justification: Section 3.3 newly explains the tradeoff between avoiding waits for slower agents and reducing communication through more exploration per round. General accommodation of unequal agent speeds was already discussed in v1 Appendix C; the mode-selection interpretation is new.

D1.justification: The retained experiments preserve iota=1, N0=200, the baseline-settings source, hardware and memory specifications, runtime statement, and supplemental-code disclosure. The new notation tables organize definitions already supplied in v1 rather than adding implementation or resource-access information.

R1.justification: Appendix B substantially expands positioning against event-triggered MARL with function approximation, including Dubey and Pentland, Min et al., and Hsu et al., distinguishing trajectory sharing from compressed statistics. It also broadens discussion of federated policy-gradient methods, inverse RL, and gap-dependent switching results.

P1.justification: The contribution summary and algorithm exposition are extensively rewritten. Section 3 separates basic structure, procedural details, and intuition; definitions are collected in Appendix A, and the main-text experiments and former speedup appendix are consolidated into Appendix C.

P2.justification: The paper adopts a different conference layout throughout, including typography, margins, headers, and algorithm formatting. It adds a round–stage schematic, two notation tables, and a four-panel experimental figure, while relocating and resizing the two unchanged experimental plots.

improvement.justification: The added wait-for-all procedure and accompanying bound substantially strengthen the paper's central communication-efficiency contribution, with an explicit waiting-time tradeoff. The reorganized explanation, schematic, and notation tables make the algorithm easier to assess, and additional simulations broaden empirical support. Validation remains limited: the largest experiment has one run, and the two synchronization modes are not directly compared empirically.
